title: Verb + -ing forms and infinitives 2
subtitle: warned everyone to stay inside / arranged for Rania to stay
summary: Decide when a verb needs an object (or a preposition + object) before a to-infinitive, and use the negative, perfect and having + past participle forms after verbs.

lesson.heading: Object before the to-infinitive - or not?

left.label: An object is necessary
left.text: In active sentences some verbs must have an object between the verb and the to-infinitive. Also: advise, allow, believe, cause, command, enable, encourage, entitle, force, invite, order, persuade, remind, show, teach, tell.
examples: The police **warned everyone to stay** inside with their windows closed.
not ~~The police warned to stay inside~~

right.label: An object is impossible
right.text: After other verbs we cannot put an object before the to-infinitive. Also: agree, consent, fail, hope, manage, offer, pretend, refuse, start, threaten, volunteer.
examples: not ~~We've decided us to leave early~~

lesson.heading: Verb + for + object + to-infinitive
lesson.text: After some verbs we have to put a preposition - usually **for** - immediately after the verb, before an object + to-infinitive. Also: advertise, campaign, long, plan, wait. After *apply* and *campaign* the to-infinitive is usually passive.

examples.text: They **arranged for Rania to stay** in London.
They **applied for** the court appearance **to be postponed**.
I waited ages **for her to come** up with some initial ideas.

lesson.heading: Other prepositions before object + to-infinitive
rows: go on, keep on, scream, shout, yell
I shouted **at the man to open** the door.
We're depending **on you to find** a solution soon.
He closed the door and signalled **to the pilot to take off**.
lesson.note: keep on at someone = talk to them about something many times; go on at someone = criticise them continually; call on someone = officially ask them to do something.

lesson.heading: Negative to-infinitives and negative -ing forms
lesson.text: Put **not** immediately before the to-infinitive or the -ing form when the reported action itself is negative. Making the main verb negative instead changes the meaning.

examples.text: We decided **not to go** to Paris after all.
examples.note: compare: The people didn't decide to go to war, it was their political leaders.

examples.text: Some of my friends have considered **not going** to college because of the cost.
examples.note: compare: I haven't considered going to college - I don't want to go on studying after school.

lesson.heading: Verb + to have + past participle
lesson.text: This form points back to an earlier event. It is common after **seem** and **appear** when we give an opinion about the past, and after passive reporting verbs such as *is / was alleged, believed, said, thought*.

examples.text: The accident **seems to have happened** at around 1 pm yesterday.
Simmons **is alleged to have assaulted** a police officer.
The prisoners **are thought to have escaped** through a broken window.

lesson.heading: Verb + having + past participle
lesson.text: With a small group of verbs the plain -ing form and **having** + past participle mean much the same thing. This happens most often with admit, deny, forget, recall, regret and remember.

examples.text: I now regret **buying** the car. = I now regret **having bought** the car.
He denies **having received** any stolen property. = He denies **receiving** any stolen property.

lesson.text: If you are unsure whether a verb takes an object, test it with *us*: *encouraged us to stay* sounds right, ~~agreed us to stay~~ does not.

exercises.prompt: My mother ___ me to throw away my old toys.
exercises.explanation: tell needs an object before the to-infinitive: told me to throw away.

exercises.prompt: My mother ___ to throw away my old toys.
exercises.explanation: threaten cannot take an object before the to-infinitive, so it fits a sentence with no object.

exercises.prompt: They ___ us to visit Riko in hospital.
exercises.explanation: allow takes an object + to-infinitive; offer and agree cannot have an object before the to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: They ___ to carry the heavy boxes up the stairs.
exercises.explanation: There is no object, so we need manage: They managed to carry the boxes.

exercises.prompt: They ___ Hamza to carry the heavy boxes up the stairs.
exercises.explanation: persuade requires an object before the to-infinitive: persuaded Hamza to carry.

exercises.prompt: Does the verb need an object before a to-infinitive, or can it never have one?
categories: Must have an object: warned everyone to stay
Cannot have an object: decided to leave

exercises.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending. Watch the preposition.

pairs.right: for employers and employees to meet next week.

pairs.left: I've learnt that you can't rely
Managers of the company have appealed
pairs.right: to workers to end their strike.
at her to do any more work on it.

exercises.prompt: When I advertised ___ a website designer for the business, Greta got the job.
exercises.explanation: advertise takes for before the object: advertise for a designer.

exercises.prompt: Report the decision. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: We decided not to go to Paris after all
exercises.explanation: not goes immediately before the to-infinitive, so the decision itself is negative.

exercises.statement: I don't recall to see him at the conference.
exercises.explanation: I don't recall seeing him at the conference. (or ... having seen him ...) recall is followed by an -ing form, not a to-infinitive.

exercises.prompt: He asked ___ as the person who donated the money.
exercises.explanation: not comes before the passive to-infinitive: asked not to be named.

exercises.prompt: I am sure my purse was on the table a few minutes ago, but now it ___.
exercises.explanation: seem + to have + past participle gives an opinion about an earlier event.
